title: POPIA — Organisational Compliance Process Flow
subtitle: Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013, POPIA Regulations (as amended), Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000 and Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020 · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells a South African private-sector organisation what it must do to comply with the Protection of Personal Information Act, by when, and who hands off to whom. It covers the standing programme (Phase 0), every new or changed processing activity (Phase 1), requests from data subjects (Phase 2), security compromises (Phase 3), dealings with the Information Regulator (Phase 4) and the annual cycle of monitoring and review (Phase 5). An employment track (E) applies the same rules to employee and applicant information, and a parallel track (P) covers events that can arise at any time. It is written for Information Officers (IOs), Deputy Information Officers (DIOs), HR, compliance and legal, IT and information security, marketing and line managers.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 ("POPIA") is fully in force. Most sections commenced on 1 July 2020 and the 12-month grace period in s.114(1) ended on 30 June 2021; ss.110 and 114(4) commenced on 30 June 2021 (Proclamation R21, GG 43461, 22 June 2020). The Regulations Relating to the Protection of Personal Information, 2018 (GN R1383, GG 42110, 14 December 2018) were amended with immediate effect on 17 April 2025 (GN 6126, GG 52523). Regulations on the processing of health information by certain responsible parties, including employers, came into force on publication on 6 March 2026 (GN 7198, GG 54268). The Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000 ("PAIA") and its 2021 Regulations (GG 45057, 27 August 2021) govern the PAIA manual and access requests. Section 54 of the Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020 (mandatory reporting to SAPS by electronic communications service providers and financial institutions) has not been put into operation (MJK, reviewed 1 July 2026; re-check before relying on this).

notes.heading: Figures in force
notes.text: Administrative fine: up to R10 million per infringement notice (s.109(2)(c)); the infringer may pay, arrange instalments or elect trial within 30 days (s.109(2)(d)), and new reg 13 (17 April 2025) sets the case-by-case affordability test for instalments. Imprisonment: up to 10 years for the s.107(a) offences, up to 12 months for the s.107(b) offences. PAIA request to a private body: decision within 30 days (s.56(1)), one extension of up to 30 days (s.57(1)). PAIA fees for private bodies: request fee R140; search and preparation R145 per hour after the first hour, capped at R435; deposit of one third where search and preparation exceed six hours (PAIA s.54; PAIA Regulations 2021, Annexure B). PAIA annual report window for private bodies: 1 April to 30 June, via the eServices portal.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LAW = Act of Parliament in force; binding now.
REG = regulation in force (POPIA Regulations as amended; health information regulations; PAIA Regulations).
GN = Information Regulator guidance note or published position; not law, but the Regulator applies it in enforcement.
CL = case law (court, year).
DRAFT = proposed or not in force; build readiness, do not treat as a current duty.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt it in policy so it binds internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: POPIA sets few hard clocks. It relies on standards such as "as soon as reasonably possible" and "appropriate, reasonable technical and organisational measures". This flow turns each standard into an internal target (BP) that is tight enough to show the Regulator a defensible process. Where the Regulator's guidance is stricter than the Act, the flow follows the guidance as policy and records the difference.

notes.heading: Seven interpretation points that shape the flow

notes.text: 1. Counting days. The amended Regulations define "day" as a calendar day, excluding a last day that falls on a Sunday or public holiday, in line with the Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 (amended reg 1). PAIA periods are also calendar days. Diarise every clock in calendar days from the day after receipt.

2. "As soon as reasonably possible". Section 22(2) sets no number of hours. It allows only for the legitimate needs of law enforcement and the steps needed to determine the scope of the compromise and restore the integrity of the system. The flow sets a BP target of 72 hours from reasonable belief to Regulator notification. Any delay beyond that needs a written reason, because the eServices notification asks for the reason for delay.

3. Responsible party, operator and group structures. Each legal entity in a group is a separate responsible party and must register its own IO and DIOs (IO guidance note, para 5.3). A vendor that processes for the organisation is an operator and needs a written s.21 contract. One KwaZulu-Natal High Court decision treated an employee as bound by s.20 operator duties (Zulu Nyala Game Ranch v Beukes, KZD 2025); that reading is novel and has not been tested on appeal.

4. Juristic persons are data subjects. "Personal information" includes information about an identifiable, existing juristic person (s.1). Supplier, client and business-to-business data are in scope, which matters for direct marketing and B2B databases.

5. Consent is one ground, not the default. Section 11(1) lists six justifications. In employment, contract (s.11(1)(b)), legal obligation (s.11(1)(c)) and legitimate interest (s.11(1)(f)) usually fit better than consent, which an employee can withdraw and which may not be freely given. Special personal information and children's information need a s.27 or s.35 authorisation as well as a s.11 ground.

6. Two access routes. A data subject asking for their own information uses POPIA s.23, but the manner of access and the refusal grounds come from PAIA (s.23(4), s.25). Treat every access request as a PAIA request to a private body for timing (30 days) unless it is a simple confirmation, which is free (s.23(1)(a)).

7. Guidance notes bind in practice. Guidance notes are not law, but the Regulator's Enforcement Committee applies them. Examples are the direct marketing guidance note (3 December 2024), which treats telephone calls as electronic communication, and the 2024 revised prior authorisation guidance. Follow them unless legal advice supports a different reading, and record the reasoning.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: Information Officer (IO, by law the head of the private body or the person they authorise in writing); Deputy Information Officer (DIO); Privacy Steering Committee (PSC); Board or EXCO (BOARD); Human Resources (HR); Line Manager (LM); Compliance and Legal (CL); Information Security Officer and IT (ISO); Marketing (MKT); Procurement and vendor management (PROC); Internal Audit (IA); Occupational health practitioner (OHS); Designated Officer under the GBS PDA flow (DO); Operator or vendor (OP); data subject (DS); Information Regulator (IR).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no trigger. It must exist before the organisation can show the Regulator that it complies, and it is the first thing the Regulator asks for in an assessment or after a compromise. The enforcement notices issued to date show the pattern. In 2023 the Department of Justice was fined R5 million because licences for its security software had lapsed (s.19; the fine is under court challenge). In 2023 Dis-Chem was ordered to put a written operator contract in place (s.21). In 2026 the Central Johannesburg TVET College was ordered to register its IO and DIOs within 31 days and to produce a compliance framework (s.8, s.55(2)). Each was a Phase 0 failure.

notes.heading: Data-subject side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed by data subjects yet. Their later rights depend on this phase: an organisation without a manual, notices or a request channel cannot show that it informed people of their rights (s.18(1)(h)) or that a request route was reasonably accessible (amended reg 2).

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: BOARD → IO (authorisation and resources). IO → IR (registration). PROC → CL (operator contracts). ISO → IO (security posture). HR → IO (employee notices and HR inventory). MKT → CL (consent design). CL → website owner (manual and notices published).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Registration is the first thing the Regulator checks and the easiest finding against an organisation. In May 2026 the Enforcement Committee ordered a college to register its IO and DIOs within 31 days, together with wider orders. Keep the eServices confirmation, and re-register promptly whenever the CEO changes, because the head of the body is the IO by operation of law.

steps.title: Confirm the IO
steps.action: The head of the private body is the IO by law (the CEO or equivalent for a company). If the head authorises someone else, do it in writing on a template substantially similar to the Regulator's Annexure C. The person should be at management level or above. The head stays accountable and may withdraw the authorisation in writing. For a multinational, authorise a person in South Africa.

source.section: §03 Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)

steps.title: Retention and destruction
steps.action: Set a retention period for each record type. Keep records only as long as needed, unless a law, contract, consent or lawful purpose requires longer (s.14(1)). Where a record was used to make a decision about a person, keep it long enough for them to request access (s.14(3)). Destroy or de-identify records so that they cannot be reconstructed (s.14(4)–(5)). Restrict rather than delete where the data subject contests accuracy or the record is needed as evidence (s.14(6)). Align with employment retention laws (track E).

steps.title: Direct marketing
steps.action: Unsolicited electronic direct marketing (email, SMS, WhatsApp, push notification, social-media DM and, in the Regulator's view, telephone calls) needs consent, or an existing customer relationship that meets s.69(3). Ask a non-customer for consent only once, on a form substantially similar to Form 4. An opt-out is not consent. Record telephone consent requests. Every message must identify the sender and give an opt-out. Keep a suppression list. Register with the National Consumer Commission's National Opt-Out Registry and screen lists against it monthly (CPA; see the GBS CPA flow).

source.section: §03 Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)

steps.title: Prior authorisation screen
steps.action: Screen the inventory for the four s.57(1) categories: (a) unique identifiers used for a different purpose and linked with information from other responsible parties; (b) information on criminal behaviour or unlawful or objectionable conduct processed on behalf of third parties; (c) credit reporting; (d) special or children's information sent to a foreign third party without adequate protection. Each needs prior authorisation once, not each time, unless the processing changes (s.57(3)). Prior authorisation is required for s.57 processing that began on or after 1 July 2021, and for further processing after that date (guidance note paras 6.1–6.2). Since 1 February 2022 such processing may not continue until the Regulator has decided (s.58(2); para 3.2). Any unauthorised processing must stop and an application must be lodged.

stages.group: Phase 1 — New processing, change and privacy impact assessment
stages.title: Phase 1 — New processing, change and privacy impact assessment
intro: Every new system, process, product, vendor, data-sharing arrangement or AI tool, and every material change to an existing one, must pass through Phase 1 before go-live. The trigger is the decision to change, not the go-live date. The Regulations require the IO to ensure that a personal information impact assessment (PIIA) is done (reg 4(1)(b)). The Regulator has said it plans a PIIA guidance note in its 2026/27 year (DRAFT; verify).

notes.heading: Data-subject obligations at this stage
notes.text: None. Data subjects receive the notice and, where consent is the ground, decide freely. They keep the right to object at any time to processing under s.11(1)(d)–(f) (s.11(3)(a)).

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: Business owner → IO (screening). IO → ISO and CL (assessment). CL → IR (prior authorisation). PROC → OP (contract). IO → GBS AI compliance flow (AI tools). IO → website owner (manual and notice update).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: The common failure is shadow procurement: staff sign up to free or low-cost cloud and AI tools with a credit card and upload customer or employee data. Block unsanctioned tools technically where possible, and make the screening form short enough that people actually use it.

steps.title: Intake and screen
steps.trigger: A project, procurement, data-sharing, analytics or AI request involving personal information.
steps.action: Business owner completes a short screening form: what data, whose, why, which system or vendor, which countries, any special or children's information, any automated decisions, any monitoring. Without a screening reference, procurement cannot raise an order (BP).

steps.trigger: Screening done.

Otherwise record a short-form assessment.

stages.title: Phase 3 — Security compromise (s.22) incident response
intro: A security compromise is any case where there are reasonable grounds to believe that personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person (s.22(1)). The trigger is reasonable grounds to believe, not proof. Ransomware, a misdirected email, a lost laptop, a staff member sharing records on WhatsApp and an operator's compromise all qualify. The Regulator expects notification through its eServices portal, which it made mandatory for compromise reports from 1 April 2025 (media statement of 7 April 2025). It reported more than 8 000 notifications to date, and more than 1 220 since its 1 April 2026 briefing (September 2026).

notes.heading: Data-subject obligations at this stage
notes.text: None by law. Data subjects are expected to act on the recommendations in the notice (change passwords, alert banks). Some may complain to the Regulator (s.74) or sue for damages (s.99, see P5).

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: Staff and OP → ISO and IO (immediate). ISO → IO (assessment). IO → IR (eServices). IO → data subjects (notice). CL → SAPS (case). HR → Misconduct flow. IO → BOARD (crisis decisions and closure report).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: The two most common enforcement findings are late or missing notification and repeated incidents with no notification at all (Lancet Laboratories, fined R100 000 and paid). An accidental cause does not remove the duty to notify (CJC TVET enforcement notice, 2026). If the organisation decides that a near-miss is not notifiable, record why. That record is the evidence in an assessment.

stages.group: Employment track — employee and applicant information (E)
stages.title: Employment track — employee and applicant information (E)
intro: Employers process more special personal information about employees than about almost anyone else: health records, biometrics, race (for employment equity), trade union membership and criminal records. The employment track applies Phases 0–3 to the employment lifecycle. It links to the GBS Resourcing (Recruitment and Selection), Performance Management, Incapacity, Misconduct, Operational Requirements, COIDA, OHSA and Off-Boarding flows.

notes.heading: Employee obligations
notes.text: Keep personal information they handle confidential and use it only for work purposes; report incidents immediately; follow the monitoring and acceptable-use policy; give accurate information and update it. A former employee who takes client lists can be interdicted (Zulu Nyala Game Ranch v Beukes, KZD 2025, where the court applied s.20 to an employee).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Do not rely on employee consent as a blanket ground. Consent can be withdrawn at any time and, in an employment relationship, may not be voluntary. Use the specific ground for each category, and keep consent for genuinely optional processing such as wellness programmes or a talent pool.

referenceTables.title: Master flow at a glance
intro: Phase 0 is permanent. Each event (a new or changed processing activity, a data-subject request, a suspected compromise) runs through its own phase. The matter enters Phase 4 only when the Regulator is involved: a prior authorisation application, a complaint, an assessment, or a s.22 notification that leads to questions. Every route closes in Phase 5, and lessons from Phase 5 change the Phase 0 controls. The employment track and the parallel events run alongside every phase.

Read each column top to bottom to see who acts in that phase. Read each lane left to right to see one party's whole job. The IO lane is the spine: every request, change and incident passes through it. Dashed lines are formal filings with the Regulator, through the eServices portal or a prescribed form. Operators never notify the Regulator for the organisation. They tell the responsible party immediately (s.21(2)), and the responsible party notifies.

intro: 1. No hard notification clock. Section 22(2) gives no number of hours. Organisations set their own targets, which makes enforcement inconsistent. A 72-hour outer limit, as in other regimes, would help.

2. Regulation 3 timing. Amended reg 3 requires notice of the action taken within 30 days "of receiving the outcome of the request". The responsible party produces the outcome itself, so the start date is unclear. This flow counts from receipt of the request.
3. Citation error in amended reg 1. The definition of "writing" refers to the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 25 of 2002 but gives the year as 2022.

4. "Approach once" for consent. Section 69(2)(b) allows one approach to request consent. The guidance note's treatment of telephone calls as electronic communication extends that limit to voice calls, which is contested and awaits Enforcement Committee decisions.

5. Personnel rules under s.33. The general authorisation for processing personnel information about criminal behaviour or biometrics refers to rules "established in compliance with labour legislation", which no instrument defines.
6. Health regulations: no transition period. The 2026 regulations applied from publication, with a broad definition of employer, and no grace period for updating contracts and HR systems.

7. Fine only after non-compliance in practice. The Regulator has said that a party that complies within the period of an enforcement notice cannot then be fined, which weakens deterrence. It is drafting amendments.

8. Pseudonymised identifiers. The matric judgment held that publishing results with examination numbers but no names was not processing of personal information. That sits uneasily with the s.1 definition, which includes "any identifying number", and is under appeal.

9. s.57(1)(a) "unique identifiers". The scope of linking identifiers "with information processed by other responsible parties" is wide enough to catch ordinary employee-number integrations with payroll bureaus. Guidance is needed.
10. No AI-specific guidance. Section 71 has no guidance, although AI recruitment and monitoring tools are spreading. The planned PIIA guidance note should cover AI.

An independent second-line review on 19 October 2026 found no Critical, 2 Major, 12 Minor and 4 Improvement findings. GBS approved all of them, and each was implemented in this version. The version number stays at v1.0.
